name: Diego Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Brightline Creative, a small agency of seven people that does packaging and labels, mostly for food brands. Jam jars, hot sauce, oat milk cartons, that kind of thing. My day is mostly in Illustrator, laying out labels to the printer's die-lines, which are the cutting shapes, and checking that the ingredients text is the right size by law. I'm the newest designer, so I get the fiddly technical jobs while Marco, the senior, does the brand ideas.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like holding the finished thing. There's a chilli sauce in the corner shop by my flat with my label on it, and I still point it out to people. What wears me out is the corrections loop, where the client's lawyer changes one word and I redo forty labels. I use an AI image tool now and then for mood boards, but only because Marco showed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, the tools were always better at hype than at packaging. A label has to fit a real jar and pass real rules. At the pub I'd say the robots can't read a food law either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief. I'm not the quickest designer and I know Marco covers for me sometimes. A slow world gives me time to catch up. I'm on decent pay for a junior and I've got eight months of rent in the bank, so I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Brightline and ask to sit in on Marco's brand meetings, because that's where the real design happens. I'd keep using the image tool for mood boards when it helps. I'd also finally put some savings into the pension my union rep keeps telling me about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored of all the hype, but calm. My work and money feel fine in that picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a union rep. Are you in a union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I joined the creative workers' union last year, after a friend got let go with one week's notice. It's small for designers but I believe in it. In this picture I'd mostly go to the socials and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the routine bits AI does take over touch your day at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the corrections loop gets faster, if software can swap ingredients across forty labels. That would honestly be lovely. It would give me back maybe a day a week, and I'd spend it learning brand work from Marco.

say: I'd say AI was always **better at hype** than at real packaging.
At the pub I'd joke that robots **can't read food law** either.
think: I'm **relieved**, because a slow world gives a slow junior time to **catch up**.
With **eight months** of rent saved and good pay, I'd be fine.
do: Ask to sit in on the senior's **brand meetings** to learn real design.
Keep using the **image tool** for mood boards when it helps.
Start paying into a **pension** from my savings.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **bored** of all the hype.
S0.quote: A label has to fit a real jar and pass real rules.
fieldNote: He sees **food labelling rules** as a natural shield against hype.
He's already a **union member**, joined after a friend lost work at a week's notice.
He'd welcome AI that cuts the **corrections loop** and frees a day a week.

steps.text: Sit in on Marco's brand meetings to learn concept work
Use the AI image tool for mood boards when useful
Start paying a monthly amount into a pension

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that we should agree as a team how we use AI, and that it should cut boring work, not people. Online I'd share the union's line on keeping juniors in the trade. If nobody trains juniors now, there won't be any seniors in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the technical half of my job goes. Die-lines, resizing, ingredients text, all of that is checking and fitting, which is exactly what software gets good at. I'd be left with the half where I'm weakest, the ideas half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly, not just for mood boards, once I saw Marco and the others doing it. I'd ask Brightline to pay for a short course in packaging concept work. I'd push the union branch to get a basic agreement on AI at small studios. And I'd save harder, maybe an extra two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I might lose the job, or it might shrink to part-time. I still feel I have some control, though, with savings and lots of agencies around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Priya? Does her job come into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya's an architect's assistant, and she does a lot of drawings and planning paperwork, so she's in the same boat. That's what makes me nervous, it's both of us at once. Her parents' rental flat, where we pay low rent, is the thing that keeps us steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools once others did. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen people waste months on tools that disappear. I'd wait until I saw it work on a real job at Brightline, maybe a client brief done in half the time. Then I'd jump in properly. I'm not the first in, but I'm not the last either.

say: I'd say AI should **cut boring work**, not people, and agree it as a **team**.
I'd share the union's line that **untrained juniors** mean no seniors later.
think: I expect the **technical half** of my job, die-lines and resizing, to go.
I'd be left with the **ideas half**, where I'm weakest.
do: Learn the **AI tools** properly once colleagues prove them on real jobs.
Ask the agency to pay for a **packaging concept** course.
Push the union branch for an **AI agreement** and save **two hundred** extra monthly.
feel: **Anxious** about a shrinking job, but feeling **some control** thanks to savings.
S1.quote: If nobody trains juniors now, there won't be any seniors in ten years.
fieldNote: His **partner's job** is exposed too, so the household risk is doubled.
He waits for **proof** on a real job before adopting tools, then commits fully.
Low rent in his **partner's parents'** flat is a hidden safety net.

steps.text: Learn Brightline's AI tools after seeing them work on a client job
Ask Brightline to pay for a packaging concept design course
Push the union branch for an AI agreement at small studios
Save an extra two hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a moment for governments to act like it's a war, with real money for people who lose their jobs. I'd be out with the union, on the street. At work I'd say let's be honest with each other about who's staying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think a junior packaging designer is gone by 2028, and my partner's drawings go too. The checking, the layout, even the concepts, AI does them better and cheaper. Priya and I would both be looking for work in the same year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop waiting for proof, for once. In the first few months I'd talk to the label printers we use, Hartley Print, about a job on the press or in finishing, because that's hands-on. I'd sit down with Priya and work out a budget on one income. And I'd be at the union's protests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at three in the morning doing sums. It feels like the floor going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does it mean for you that robots for hands-on work come three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the printer's floor is the safe spot until about 2031. So I'd get on it fast, learn to run a press, and earn while I can. But I'd know I'm buying three years, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, honestly. We barely use it and it's eating money. Then the trips to see my cousins abroad, which hurts. I'd keep the union dues, though.

say: I'd say governments must treat it **like a war**, with real money for workers.
At work I'd want **honesty** about who's staying.
think: I think a **junior packaging designer** is gone by 2028.
My partner's **drawing work** goes too, in the **same year** as mine.
do: Ask **Hartley Print** for press or finishing work within months.
Sell **the car** and cut trips abroad to run on **one income**.
Join the union's **protests** for support money.
S2.quote: A junior packaging designer is gone by 2028, and my partner's drawings go too.
fieldNote: Facing speed, he drops his usual **wait for proof** habit.
He sees the press floor as **three years bought**, not a career.
Both **household incomes** fall at once, which drives the alarm.

steps.text: Ask Hartley Print for a job on the press or finishing
Sell the car and cut trips abroad to see cousins
March with the union for income support for workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I'd say let's use them. Retraining money, a fair deal for juniors, a plan for the trade. I'd say it at union meetings and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still lose the design job by 2031. But five years is enough to get a trade, and that's the difference between scared and alarmed for me. I'd have some say in where I land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Brightline two or three more years and save hard. Meanwhile I'd learn print finishing at Hartley on Saturdays. And Priya and I would talk about whether one of us retrains in something hands-on, like her going into site surveying, which is out in the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frantic. I can see a path, even if I don't love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the hands-on work take you after robots arrive around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I won't pretend I do. Maybe by then there's a support scheme or a shorter week. I'd want the union to have fought for something before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep learning the AI tools in the meantime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because if they make Brightline faster for a couple of years, I'd keep my job longer. Using the AI tool that replaces you is a bit sad, but money's money. I'd rather leave on my own terms.

say: I'd say **use the five years** for retraining money and a fair deal.
I'd raise it at **union meetings** and at work.
think: I'd still **lose the design job** by 2031.
Five years is enough to **get a trade**, so I'd have some say.
do: Stay at the agency **two or three years** and save hard.
Learn **print finishing** at the printer on Saturdays.
Keep using the **AI tools** to stay useful longer.
feel: **Anxious** but not frantic, because he can see **a path**.
S3.quote: Using the AI tool that replaces you is a bit sad, but money's money.
fieldNote: The five years turns his alarm into **planning**.
He's honest he **doesn't know** what follows robots around 2034.
He'd use AI tools **pragmatically** to stay employed longer, despite misgivings.

steps.text: Stay at Brightline two or three years and save hard
Learn print finishing at Hartley Print on Saturdays
Use Brightline's AI tools to stay useful until 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time to plan fairly, if politicians actually do it. I'd vote for whoever offers retraining funds and a shorter week. At work I'd be the one asking what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 37 by 2036. That's young enough to have a whole second career. My worry is drifting, staying at Brightline because it's comfortable, then waking up in 2035 with nothing new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set myself a rule: by 30, I'm in something hands-on or partly hands-on. Maybe print production, maybe exhibition building. I'd put money into a course, maybe two thousand, and keep saving. And I'd keep being active in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. It's the same end, but I'd have time to steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why set a rule by 30?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know myself. I wait until something's proven, and with ten years, nothing's proven until it's too late. A date makes me act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your friends who are designers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them not to wait until AI takes their job before they start learning something new. Most of them would laugh, because they're good. I'm not, yet, so maybe that makes it easier for me to leave.

say: I'd say a **decade is plenty** if politicians actually plan fairly.
I'd vote for **retraining funds** and a shorter week.
think: I'd be **37** in 2036, young enough for a second career.
My worry is **drifting** at a comfortable job until it's too late.
do: Set a **deadline of 30** to be in hands-on or partly hands-on work.
Spend about **two thousand** on a print production or exhibition-building course.
Stay active in the **union** and keep saving.
S4.quote: I wait until something's proven, and with ten years, nothing's proven until it's too late.
fieldNote: He sets a **personal deadline** to beat his own habit of waiting.
Being a **weaker junior** makes leaving design feel easier to him.
He keeps **union and voting** at the centre of his response.

steps.text: Move into print production or exhibition building by age 30
Spend about two thousand on a hands-on production course
Vote for parties offering retraining funds and shorter weeks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because Priya and I lose our jobs in the same year. What would help is income support while we retrain, something like half a salary for a year. And a printer or a workshop that's paid to take on people like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the corner shop. I meant it about the chilli sauce label. I'd miss seeing my work on a shelf more than I'd miss the money.
